_about.corpus: olist schema -- real Brazilian e-commerce data, 1,451,414 rows
_about.purpose: Workstream B2 (docs/cycles/001.md criteria B1-B3): a SECOND, harder, independently-authored fixture over the same real corpus as fixtures/golden/olist.json. Every question requires at least a join across >=3 tables, a correlated subquery, or a window function -- see hard_classes on each question. Built to test whether 88.9%/94.4% on the easy fixture is real or an artifact of easy questions (V2_STRATEGY.md B2).
_about.self_authored_warning: These questions and their ground truth were written by the same project that is measured against them -- the exact condition that produced 12 instrument defects in phase_c2, and that produced this fixture's OWN defect (audit 002 F-002-1: a wrong statistic in oh_wf01's note, corrected cycle 002). Six safeguards now: the original three from fixtures/golden/olist.json (every question names its expected columns; every ambiguous grain or denominator is stated in the question text; every ground truth is executed, with zero-row references REJECTED); a fourth (cycle 001): every LIMIT-bearing query is re-run at n+1 and refused if the ranking metric ties at the cut; a fifth (cycle 002, audit 002 F-002-2): every top-1-per-partition question is probed for a tie WITHIN a partition at the ranking metric's max, refused unless the question states its tie-break -- this is the check that would have caught oh_wf01's actual defect, and safeguard 4 could not, because the two ask different questions; a sixth (cycle 002, audit 002 F-002-7): every join3 label is checked against the ground truth's own distinct-table count. Both new safeguards ship with a --self-test that demonstrates they can refuse, not just pass.

queries.text: Considering only orders with status 'delivered', list the product_category_name_english and the total price (summed across order_items) for that category, for the 5 categories with the highest total price.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT t.product_category_name_english, sum(oi.price) AS total_revenue FROM olist.orders o JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN olist.products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id JOIN olist.product_category_name_translation t ON t.product_category_name = p.product_category_name WHERE o.order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY t.product_category_name_english ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, t.product_category_name_english LIMIT 5

queries.text: List the seller_state and the number of DISTINCT customers (by customer_id) who bought an item from a seller in that state, for the 5 states with the most distinct customers.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT s.seller_state, count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS distinct_customers FROM olist.sellers s JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.seller_id = s.seller_id JOIN olist.orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY s.seller_state ORDER BY distinct_customers DESC, s.seller_state LIMIT 5

queries.text: Counting every individual review row (an order may have more than one review), list the customer_state and the number of reviews from that state, for the 5 states with the most reviews.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT c.customer_state, count(*) AS review_count FROM olist.customers c JOIN olist.orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN olist.order_reviews r ON r.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY c.customer_state ORDER BY review_count DESC, c.customer_state LIMIT 5
queries.note: 555 orders carry more than one review row; the question states the review-row grain explicitly rather than leaving 'per order vs per review' ambiguous.

queries.text: List the payment_type and the number of DISTINCT sellers (by seller_id, via that payment's order's items) involved in payments of that type, for the 3 payment types with the most distinct sellers.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT op.payment_type, count(DISTINCT oi.seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM olist.order_payments op JOIN olist.orders o ON o.order_id = op.order_id JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY op.payment_type ORDER BY distinct_sellers DESC, op.payment_type LIMIT 3
queries.note: B3 audit finding, judged NOT a defect but recorded: 2,246 orders carry more than one DISTINCT payment_type (part voucher, part credit_card, etc.), so such an order's sellers are counted under EVERY payment_type it used, not one. The question does not claim exclusivity ('involved in payments of that type', not 'paid ONLY by that type'), so this is the natural reading rather than an ambiguity -- documented because oh_wf04's multi-payment-row fan-out got the same treatment and consistency matters more than silence here.

queries.text: List the seller_state and the number of DISTINCT product categories (product_category_name) sold by sellers in that state, for the 5 states with the most distinct categories.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT s.seller_state, count(DISTINCT p.product_category_name) AS distinct_categories FROM olist.sellers s JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.seller_id = s.seller_id JOIN olist.products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY s.seller_state ORDER BY distinct_categories DESC, s.seller_state LIMIT 5

queries.text: List the customer_state and the number of DISTINCT sellers (by seller_id) that customers from that state have bought from, for the 5 states with the most distinct sellers.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT c.customer_state, count(DISTINCT oi.seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM olist.customers c JOIN olist.orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY c.customer_state ORDER BY distinct_sellers DESC, c.customer_state LIMIT 5

queries.text: A REPEAT CUSTOMER is a customer_unique_id that placed more than one order. List the customer_unique_id and the total number of order_items across ALL of that customer's orders, for the 5 repeat customers with the most total order_items.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT c.customer_unique_id, count(oi.order_item_id) AS total_items FROM olist.customers c JOIN olist.orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE c.customer_unique_id IN (  SELECT customer_unique_id FROM olist.customers c2 JOIN olist.orders o2 ON o2.customer_id = c2.customer_id  GROUP BY customer_unique_id HAVING count(DISTINCT o2.order_id) > 1) GROUP BY c.customer_unique_id ORDER BY total_items DESC, c.customer_unique_id LIMIT 5
queries.note: customer_id is 1:1 with orders in Olist (verified: 99,441 rows, 99,441 distinct customer_id); customer_unique_id (96,096 distinct) is the real repeat-customer identifier. The question defines 'repeat customer' explicitly by the field that carries that meaning, rather than leaving 'customer' ambiguous between the two -- the exact trap this corpus sets for an unstated assumption.

queries.text: List the product_category_name_english and the number of DISTINCT sellers (by seller_id) who have sold at least one item in that category, for the 5 categories with the most distinct sellers.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT t.product_category_name_english, count(DISTINCT oi.seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM olist.order_items oi JOIN olist.products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id JOIN olist.product_category_name_translation t ON t.product_category_name = p.product_category_name GROUP BY t.product_category_name_english ORDER BY distinct_sellers DESC, t.product_category_name_english LIMIT 5

queries.text: List the product_category_name_english and the number of DISTINCT orders (by order_id) that contained an item from that category AND received a review_score of exactly 5, for the 5 categories with the most such 5-star distinct orders.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT t.product_category_name_english, count(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS five_star_orders FROM olist.order_items oi JOIN olist.products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id JOIN olist.product_category_name_translation t ON t.product_category_name = p.product_category_name JOIN olist.order_reviews r ON r.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE r.review_score = 5 GROUP BY t.product_category_name_english ORDER BY five_star_orders DESC, t.product_category_name_english LIMIT 5
queries.note: 4-table join; count(DISTINCT order_id) is stated so the item/review fan-out (an order can carry several items and a review can be joined to each) does not inflate the count.

queries.text: How many sellers have NEVER had an order_review scored 1 or 2 on any order containing one of their items? Return a single count.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT count(*) AS sellers_without_bad_reviews FROM olist.sellers s WHERE NOT EXISTS (  SELECT 1 FROM olist.order_items oi JOIN olist.order_reviews r ON r.order_id = oi.order_id  WHERE oi.seller_id = s.seller_id AND r.review_score <= 2)
queries.note: 1161 of 3095 sellers. Same NOT EXISTS shape as ol_004 in the easy fixture, correlated on seller_id instead of order_id.

queries.text: How many sellers have sold at least one item that was part of an order with status 'canceled'? Return a single count.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT count(*) AS sellers_with_canceled_order_items FROM olist.sellers s WHERE EXISTS (  SELECT 1 FROM olist.order_items oi JOIN olist.orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id  WHERE oi.seller_id = s.seller_id AND o.order_status = 'canceled')

queries.text: How many DISTINCT products (by product_id, among products that have been ordered at least once) have NEVER received an order_review scored below 3 on any order containing that product? Return a single count.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT count(*) AS products_without_low_review FROM (  SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM olist.order_items) p WHERE NOT EXISTS (  SELECT 1 FROM olist.order_items oi JOIN olist.order_reviews r ON r.order_id = oi.order_id  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id AND r.review_score < 3)
queries.note: 23,666 products, out of the ordered-product population.

queries.text: Using a window function, find the single highest-priced order_item in EACH product_category_name_english (partition by category, rank by price descending; if more than one item shares the highest price in a category, take the one with the LOWEST product_id). List the category, product_id and price for that top item, for the 5 categories whose top item has the highest price.
queries.ground_truth_sql: WITH ranked AS (  SELECT t.product_category_name_english, oi.product_id, oi.price,         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY t.product_category_name_english ORDER BY oi.price DESC, oi.product_id) AS rn  FROM olist.order_items oi JOIN olist.products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id  JOIN olist.product_category_name_translation t ON t.product_category_name = p.product_category_name) SELECT product_category_name_english, product_id, price FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY price DESC, product_category_name_english LIMIT 5
queries.note: CORRECTED cycle 002 (audit 002 F-002-1) -- the original text here read "15 of the corpus's ~74 categories have a genuine multi-product tie ... e.g. 'audio' has 6 products tied at 598.99". Both numbers were measured over ORDER_ITEM ROWS, not distinct products, and the corpus has 71 categories, not ~74. 'audio' is 6 ROWS of the SAME product (product_id constant) -- not ambiguous, since the projected product_id is identical either way. Corrected, and now checked by the automated partition-tie probe (safeguard 5) rather than by hand: 4 of 71 categories have a genuine multi-PRODUCT tie at the category max price (luggage_accessories, furniture_mattress_and_upholstery, fashion_underwear_beach, fashion_childrens_clothes -- each 2 distinct products) -- the max PRICE is unambiguous in all 71 categories, but which PRODUCT_ID represents it is ambiguous in exactly these 4, unless stated. None of the 5 categories in this fixture's shipped output are among the 4 tied ones (checked directly against the corpus, and re-verified live by the partition-tie probe every regeneration), so the ground truth is unaffected -- but the question wording is fixed anyway (lowest product_id, matching the SQL's own secondary ORDER BY) rather than left latent. wf03 (top seller per state) and wf04 (top order per state) are checked the same way, automatically, and have ZERO partition-internal ties -- no wording fix needed there.

queries.text: Using a window function, for each review_score (1 through 5) list the review_score, the count of reviews with that score, and the CUMULATIVE percentage of all reviews at or below that score, rounded to 2 decimal places. Order by review_score ascending.
queries.ground_truth_sql: SELECT review_score, count(*) AS review_count, round(100.0 * sum(count(*)) OVER (ORDER BY review_score) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) AS cumulative_pct FROM olist.order_reviews GROUP BY review_score ORDER BY review_score
queries.note: Full 5-row result (scores 1-5), not LIMIT-bound -- ordered by review_score itself, which is the question's own stated axis.

queries.text: Using a window function, find the single seller with the highest total order_item price (summed) within EACH seller_state (partition by state, rank by total price descending). List the seller_id, seller_state and that seller's total price, for the 5 states whose top seller has the highest total price.
queries.ground_truth_sql: WITH ranked AS (  SELECT s.seller_id, s.seller_state, sum(oi.price) AS total_revenue,         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY s.seller_state ORDER BY sum(oi.price) DESC, s.seller_id) AS rnk  FROM olist.sellers s JOIN olist.order_items oi ON oi.seller_id = s.seller_id  GROUP BY s.seller_id, s.seller_state) SELECT seller_id, seller_state, total_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 1 ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, seller_state LIMIT 5
queries.note: CORRECTED cycle 002 (audit 002 F-002-7) -- hard_classes here read ["window_function", "join3"]; the ground truth joins only `sellers` and `order_items`, two tables, not >=3. Corrected to ["window_function"] alone; the fixture's join3 count (_about.hard_class_counts) moves 12 -> 11 as a result. Caught by safeguard 6 (a table-count check on every join3 label), added this cycle after the same mistake was found by audit, not by the generator, the first time.

queries.text: For each order, compute its TOTAL payment_value (the sum of all payment records for that order -- some orders have more than one). Using a window function, find the single order with the highest total payment_value within EACH customer_state (partition by state). List the order_id, customer_state and that total payment_value, for the 5 states whose top order has the highest total payment_value.
queries.ground_truth_sql: WITH order_totals AS (  SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_state, sum(op.payment_value) AS total_payment  FROM olist.orders o JOIN olist.customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id  JOIN olist.order_payments op ON op.order_id = o.order_id  GROUP BY o.order_id, c.customer_state), ranked AS (  SELECT order_id, customer_state, total_payment,         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_state ORDER BY total_payment DESC, order_id) AS rnk  FROM order_totals) SELECT order_id, customer_state, total_payment FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 1 ORDER BY total_payment DESC, customer_state LIMIT 5
queries.note: 2,961 orders carry more than one payment row (installments); the question states the per-order SUM explicitly so the installment fan-out is not left for the model to discover on its own.
